stem:
You are the consultation liaison psychiatry registrar reviewing a 27 year old woman on the general medical ward for immobility and reduced oral intake over the last 3 days. Her mother reports 6 months of increasing withdrawal, disorganised speech, and 2 recent psychiatric admissions for a first-episode psychosis for which she has been on olanzapine 20 mg nightly. Two weeks ago she was commenced on lorazepam-free treatment escalation with haloperidol added at 5 mg daily.

On examination she is mute, holds her left arm elevated when passively placed and maintains that posture, and she resists passive limb movement in a way that varies with speed of movement. She has a fixed staring gaze. Vital signs: pulse 98/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent in room air, temperature 37.1 degrees Celsius. Investigations: creatine kinase 380 U/L (under 200), sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, urea 6.8 mmol/L, TSH normal, and CT head is unremarkable. Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale is 12.

data_table.History: 6 months worsening withdrawal and disorganised speech; olanzapine 20 mg plus haloperidol 5 mg for 2 weeks
data_table.Vitals: HR 98; BP 118/74; RR 16; SpO2 99 percent; T 37.1
data_table.Examination: Mute; waxy flexibility on passive movement; posturing left arm; gegenhalten; fixed stare
data_table.Investigations: CK 380; Na 138; K 4.2; urea 6.8; TSH normal; CT head unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate diagnostic and therapeutic step?

options.text: Commence intravenous dantrolene 2 mg/kg for suspected neuroleptic malignant syndrome as first-line
options.rationale: NMS requires hyperthermia, rigidity, autonomic instability, and marked CK elevation; this patient has none of those, and dantrolene is not first-line for catatonia (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia and Related Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia and Related Disorders

options.text: Increase haloperidol to 10 mg daily to control the underlying psychosis before any other treatment step
options.rationale: Antipsychotics can worsen catatonia and precipitate neuroleptic malignant syndrome; escalating haloperidol without a lorazepam trial is potentially harmful (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia and Related Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia and Related Disorders

options.text: Administer intramuscular lorazepam 2 mg challenge and reassess the Bush-Francis rating scale in 30 minutes
options.rationale: Catatonia is confirmed by response to a lorazepam challenge (typically 2 mg IM or IV with a 50 percent reduction on Bush-Francis within 30 minutes); this diagnostic step doubles as the first therapeutic step and precedes ECT if no response (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia and Related Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia and Related Disorders

options.text: Arrange urgent electroconvulsive therapy today before any pharmacological trial for catatonia
options.rationale: ECT is highly effective for catatonia but is reserved for lorazepam non-response or malignant catatonia; the sequential step is lorazepam trial first (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia and Related Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia and Related Disorders

options.text: Perform lumbar puncture to exclude autoimmune encephalitis before starting any specific therapy today
options.rationale: Autoimmune encephalitis (e.g. anti-NMDAR) should be considered in the workup but should not delay the lorazepam trial that both diagnoses and treats catatonia; investigations run in parallel (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia and Related Disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia and Related Disorders

explanation.summary: Catatonia is defined by mutism, immobility, waxy flexibility, posturing, negativism, staring, and gegenhalten; 2 or more Bush-Francis items are diagnostic. The immediate step is a lorazepam challenge (2 mg IM or IV) with reassessment at 30 minutes; a marked improvement confirms the diagnosis and starts treatment. Ongoing lorazepam is titrated (often up to 8 to 24 mg daily) with ECT for non-responders or malignant catatonia. Antipsychotics are minimised or held because they can worsen catatonia and precipitate NMS. Autoimmune workup (anti-NMDAR) is prudent when the picture is atypical or refractory.
key_points: Bush-Francis 2 or more items is diagnostic; lorazepam 2 mg challenge is first-line
Ongoing lorazepam titrated to 8 to 24 mg daily; ECT if no response
Antipsychotics held or minimised because they can worsen catatonia and provoke NMS
explanation.pearls: Malignant catatonia (fever, autonomic instability, rigidity, high CK) is a psychiatric emergency and progresses to ECT within 24 to 48 hours if lorazepam fails.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guidelines for Schizophrenia and Related Disorders

subtopic_detail: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose ECG interpretation and sodium bicarbonate threshold
stem:
You are the emergency medicine registrar reviewing a 34 year old woman brought in by ambulance 90 minutes after an intentional overdose of about 3 g of amitriptyline. She was found drowsy at home and gave the drug history en route. She has a background of major depressive disorder, and has recently been changed from sertraline to amitriptyline for chronic pain. She takes no other medication and drank no alcohol today.

On arrival she is drowsy but rousable and orientated when awake. Vital signs: pulse 130/min, blood pressure 92/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 96 percent, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius. ECG shows sinus tachycardia with a QRS duration of 140 ms and a tall R wave in aVR of 5 mm. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.34, PaCO2 32 mmHg, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 3.8 mmol/L, lactate 3.2 mmol/L, glucose 5.8 mmol/L. Activated charcoal was declined at scene.

data_table.Ingestion: About 3 g amitriptyline 90 minutes ago; no coingestants; drowsy but rousable
data_table.Vitals: HR 130; BP 92/56; RR 20; SpO2 96 percent; T 36.8
data_table.ECG: Sinus tachycardia; QRS duration 140 ms; R wave in aVR 5 mm
data_table.ABG: pH 7.34; PaCO2 32; HCO3 18; Na 138; K 3.8; lactate 3.2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Start intravenous amiodarone 300 mg for the tachycardia and to prevent ventricular arrhythmia
options.rationale: Class Ia and III antiarrhythmics prolong the QT and worsen sodium-channel blockade in TCA toxicity; sodium bicarbonate is the antiarrhythmic in this context, not amiodarone (Source: Australian College of Emergency Medicine Toxicology Guidelines).
source_refs: Australian College of Emergency Medicine Toxicology Guidelines

options.text: Administer activated charcoal 1 g/kg orally as her level of consciousness permits
options.rationale: Activated charcoal at 90 minutes post-ingestion in a drowsy patient without a protected airway risks aspiration and provides little benefit; airway protection is not adequate for a drowsy woman and cardiotoxicity is the immediate threat (Source: Australian College of Emergency Medicine Toxicology Guidelines).
source_refs: Australian College of Emergency Medicine Toxicology Guidelines

options.text: Give a 20 percent intralipid emulsion 1.5 mL/kg bolus as first-line therapy for the overdose
options.rationale: Intralipid is a rescue therapy for lipophilic drug cardiotoxicity when standard treatment fails; sodium bicarbonate is first-line for TCA overdose and intralipid is not initial therapy (Source: Australian College of Emergency Medicine Toxicology Guidelines).
source_refs: Australian College of Emergency Medicine Toxicology Guidelines

options.text: Administer intravenous flumazenil 0.2 mg for the reduced level of consciousness
options.rationale: Flumazenil is contraindicated in TCA overdose because it can precipitate seizures in mixed TCA-benzodiazepine ingestion and does not reverse TCA toxicity (Source: Australian College of Emergency Medicine Toxicology Guidelines).
source_refs: Australian College of Emergency Medicine Toxicology Guidelines

options.text: Give sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg intravenously and titrate serum pH to 7.5
options.rationale: QRS 100 ms or more and R wave in aVR 3 mm or more predict TCA cardiotoxicity; sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg IV bolus with pH target 7.45 to 7.55 reverses sodium-channel blockade and is the first-line treatment for TCA toxicity per AU toxicology guidance (Source: Australian College of Emergency Medicine Toxicology Guidelines).
source_refs: Australian College of Emergency Medicine Toxicology Guidelines

explanation.summary: TCA overdose kills through sodium-channel blockade producing QRS widening, hypotension, seizures, and ventricular arrhythmia. ECG features that predict toxicity are a QRS of 100 ms or more, R wave in aVR of 3 mm or more, and an R/S ratio in aVR of 0.7 or more. Treatment is sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg IV bolus with a pH target of 7.45 to 7.55, repeated as needed, plus intubation for airway protection, benzodiazepines for seizures, and fluid or vasopressors for hypotension. Class Ia, Ic, and III antiarrhythmics are contraindicated. Intralipid is rescue therapy for refractory cardiotoxicity, not first-line.
key_points: QRS 100 ms or more or R wave in aVR 3 mm or more triggers sodium bicarbonate in TCA overdose
Target pH 7.45 to 7.55 with 1 to 2 mmol/kg IV bicarbonate boluses
Avoid flumazenil and Class Ia/Ic/III antiarrhythmics; use intralipid only as rescue
explanation.pearls: The R wave in aVR is easier to measure than the QRS in an untidy trace; a tall R in aVR alone is a valid trigger to alkalinise.

sources.label: Australian College of Emergency Medicine Toxicology Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Sodium valproate teratogenicity and pregnancy-prevention program
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 26 year old woman with bipolar I disorder in remission on sodium valproate 1000 mg daily and quetiapine 100 mg nightly for 2 years. She reports 6 months of stable mood without hypomanic or depressive symptoms. She now tells you that her partner and she have started trying for a pregnancy 8 weeks ago and she does not want to change medications because 'nothing has ever worked as well'.

She has no other medical history. She is using no contraception. Her last menstrual period was 2 weeks ago and a home pregnancy test today is negative. She has full capacity for the discussion, understands she is in remission, and has an existing psychiatric care plan and mental health team engagement. She is currently on the state sodium valproate pregnancy-prevention program.

data_table.Diagnosis and history: Bipolar I in remission 6 months; stable on valproate 1000 mg plus quetiapine 100 mg for 2 years
data_table.Reproductive intent: Actively trying to conceive; no contraception; LMP 2 weeks ago; pregnancy test negative today
data_table.Program status: Enrolled in state sodium valproate pregnancy-prevention program
data_table.Insight: Full capacity; aware of remission; declines medication change

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her care?

options.text: Recommend cross-titration off valproate to lithium or lamotrigine and effective contraception until switch is complete
options.rationale: Sodium valproate carries a 10 percent major congenital malformation rate and 30 to 40 percent risk of neurodevelopmental disorders; RANZCP and TGA-mandated pregnancy prevention programs require withdrawal wherever safe, with a cross-titration to lithium or lamotrigine and continued contraception until the switch is complete (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Guidelines).
source_refs: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Guidelines

options.text: Continue valproate at the same dose and add high-dose folate 5 mg daily as adequate teratogen prevention
options.rationale: Folate supplementation does not offset the intrinsic teratogenic and neurodevelopmental risks of valproate; TGA and RANZCP mandate switching where possible in women who could become pregnant, not continuation with folate (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Guidelines).
source_refs: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Guidelines

options.text: Stop valproate today without a substitute mood stabiliser and monitor mood clinically for the next 4 weeks
options.rationale: Abrupt discontinuation without a replacement mood stabiliser carries a high relapse risk in bipolar I disorder; cross-titration protects mood stability while removing teratogen exposure (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Guidelines).
source_refs: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Guidelines

options.text: Reduce valproate to 500 mg daily as a lower teratogenic dose while she attempts to conceive
options.rationale: There is no safe teratogenic dose of valproate; reducing dose reduces but does not eliminate risk and is not an acceptable strategy when a switch is possible (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Guidelines).
source_refs: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Guidelines

options.text: Continue valproate and refer for cognitive behavioural therapy as the sole added support during conception
options.rationale: Psychological therapy does not neutralise valproate teratogenicity; continuing valproate while trying to conceive is not consistent with the program she is enrolled in (Source: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Guidelines).
source_refs: RANZCP Perinatal Mental Health Guidelines

explanation.summary: Sodium valproate has the highest teratogenicity of the AU-available anticonvulsants and mood stabilisers, with a 10 percent major malformation rate (neural tube defects, cardiac, facial) and a 30 to 40 percent rate of impaired neurodevelopmental outcome. TGA mandates a pregnancy prevention program for all women of reproductive potential prescribed valproate. When conception is planned, cross-titration to lithium (with careful monitoring) or lamotrigine (with slow titration) is the standard, with effective contraception maintained until the switch is complete and the woman is stable on the new regimen for at least 3 months.
key_points: Valproate: 10 percent major malformation; 30 to 40 percent neurodevelopmental risk
TGA pregnancy prevention program mandates alternative therapy in women who could conceive
Cross-titrate to lithium or lamotrigine with contraception until switch is complete
explanation.pearls: Lamotrigine dose needs to be increased through pregnancy because glucuronidation clearance rises; lithium dose needs monitoring across trimesters because renal clearance rises then falls postpartum.

sources.label: TGA Sodium Valproate Pregnancy Prevention Program

subtopic_detail: NSTEMI antiplatelet regimen selection in an older patient
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 78 year old man with new-onset chest pain lasting 4 hours and a high-sensitivity troponin I of 78 ng/L (99th percentile 34) that rose to 220 ng/L 3 hours later. He has known chronic kidney disease with an eGFR of 42 mL/min/1.73 m2, hypertension on perindopril, and takes no antiplatelet at baseline. He weighs 74 kg. He is not on anticoagulation and has no history of intracranial haemorrhage or recent bleeding.

On examination he is comfortable in bed with resolved chest discomfort. Vital signs: pulse 78/min, blood pressure 138/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97 percent in room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius. ECG shows sinus rhythm with 1 mm ST depression in leads V4 to V6 that has resolved on the current tracing. He has been given aspirin 300 mg and sublingual GTN and the cardiology team has planned a coronary angiogram within 24 hours.

data_table.ECG: Sinus rhythm; 1 mm ST depression V4 to V6, resolved on current
data_table.Given so far: Aspirin 300 mg; sublingual GTN; angiography planned within 24 hours
data_table.Bleeding risk: No ICH history; no recent bleeding; not on anticoagulant

lead_in: What is the most appropriate additional antiplatelet to add now?

options.text: Continue aspirin monotherapy without adding a P2Y12 inhibitor before angiography
options.rationale: Dual antiplatelet therapy is standard for NSTEMI to reduce recurrent ischaemic events; single antiplatelet under-treats when angiography is planned within 24 hours (Source: CSANZ Acute Coronary Syndrome Guidelines).
source_refs: CSANZ Acute Coronary Syndrome Guidelines

options.text: Oral prasugrel 60 mg loading dose then 10 mg daily as second antiplatelet
options.rationale: Prasugrel is contraindicated in patients over 75 years and in those with previous stroke or TIA; it is not appropriate here (Source: CSANZ Acute Coronary Syndrome Guidelines).
source_refs: CSANZ Acute Coronary Syndrome Guidelines

options.text: Oral ticagrelor 180 mg loading dose then 90 mg twice daily as second antiplatelet
options.rationale: Ticagrelor is more potent but has a higher bleeding rate in older patients and its dyspnoea and bradycardia adverse effects are more troublesome in this age group; clopidogrel is preferred over 75 (Source: CSANZ Acute Coronary Syndrome Guidelines).
source_refs: CSANZ Acute Coronary Syndrome Guidelines

options.text: Commence oral apixaban 5 mg twice daily as an anticoagulant addition to aspirin
options.rationale: DOAC monotherapy is not indicated in NSTEMI without atrial fibrillation and adds bleeding without ACS benefit; P2Y12 inhibitor is the standard second antiplatelet (Source: CSANZ Acute Coronary Syndrome Guidelines).
source_refs: CSANZ Acute Coronary Syndrome Guidelines

options.text: Oral clopidogrel 300 mg loading dose then 75 mg daily as part of dual antiplatelet therapy
options.rationale: In NSTEMI planned for angiography in a patient over 75 with reduced renal function, clopidogrel is preferred over ticagrelor and prasugrel because both carry higher bleeding risk in older patients (prasugrel contraindicated over 75 kg cut-off aside, and ticagrelor has higher intracranial haemorrhage in over 75s); clopidogrel is the CSANZ-preferred agent when bleeding risk is high (Source: CSANZ Acute Coronary Syndrome Guidelines).
source_refs: CSANZ Acute Coronary Syndrome Guidelines

explanation.summary: For NSTEMI in a patient over 75 with reduced renal function, dual antiplatelet therapy is standard alongside heparin bridging to angiography. CSANZ prefers clopidogrel over ticagrelor or prasugrel in older patients because both alternatives carry higher rates of intracranial and gastrointestinal bleeding in over-75s; prasugrel is explicitly contraindicated over 75 years, in patients under 60 kg, and after prior stroke or TIA. Ticagrelor also has dyspnoea and bradycardia effects that are less well tolerated in older patients. Aspirin monotherapy is not adequate before planned coronary angiography for NSTEMI.
key_points: Clopidogrel is preferred P2Y12 inhibitor over 75 years or with high bleeding risk
Prasugrel is contraindicated over 75 years, under 60 kg, or after prior stroke or TIA
Dual antiplatelet plus anticoagulant bridge is standard for NSTEMI before angiography
explanation.pearls: Older patients are the group where the theoretical superiority of ticagrelor is most likely to be undone by bleeding; the CSANZ default is clopidogrel unless there is a specific reason to escalate.

subtopic_detail: SGLT2 inhibitor indication in chronic kidney disease with albuminuria
stem:
You are the nephrology registrar reviewing a 62 year old man in the CKD clinic with type 2 diabetes for 12 years, hypertension, and a background of chronic kidney disease. His HbA1c is 7.6 percent on metformin 2 g daily and gliclazide 60 mg daily. He is on perindopril 8 mg daily and rosuvastatin 20 mg. His weight has been stable and his blood pressure is controlled.

Investigations today: eGFR 38 mL/min/1.73 m2 (stable over 12 months), urinary albumin-creatinine ratio 62 mg/mmol (up from 42 six months ago), sodium 140 mmol/L, potassium 4.4 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, HbA1c 7.6 percent (target under 7 for this patient). He has never had diabetic ketoacidosis and has no history of recurrent genital or urinary infections. Ophthalmology screening at 6 months was normal.

data_table.Current meds: Metformin 2 g/day; gliclazide 60 mg/day; perindopril 8 mg; rosuvastatin 20 mg
data_table.Renal function: eGFR 38 mL/min/1.73 m2 stable; uACR 62 mg/mmol rising from 42
data_table.Screening: No DKA history; no recurrent genital or urinary infection; ophthalmology normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next medication change?

options.text: Reduce metformin to 500 mg twice daily because of the reduced eGFR
options.rationale: Metformin can be continued at reduced dose down to eGFR 30 (500 mg twice daily), but the eGFR here is 38 and standard dose is acceptable with ongoing monitoring; this is not the priority medication change (Source: KHA-CARI SGLT2 Inhibitor Guidance in Chronic Kidney Disease).
source_refs: KHA-CARI SGLT2 Inhibitor Guidance in Chronic Kidney Disease

options.text: Add oral empagliflozin 10 mg daily as an SGLT2 inhibitor for cardiorenal protection
options.rationale: Australian KHA and CSANZ guidance recommends SGLT2 inhibitors in T2DM with eGFR 20 or above with albuminuria (uACR at least 2.5 in men or 3.5 in women) for cardiorenal benefit; empagliflozin can be initiated down to eGFR 20 and continued to dialysis (Source: KHA-CARI SGLT2 Inhibitor Guidance in Chronic Kidney Disease).
source_refs: KHA-CARI SGLT2 Inhibitor Guidance in Chronic Kidney Disease

options.text: Increase gliclazide to 120 mg daily to further lower HbA1c to under 7 percent
options.rationale: Sulphonylurea intensification adds hypoglycaemia risk in reduced eGFR without cardiorenal benefit; SGLT2 inhibitor is the intervention that improves both glycaemia and kidney outcomes (Source: KHA-CARI SGLT2 Inhibitor Guidance in Chronic Kidney Disease).
source_refs: KHA-CARI SGLT2 Inhibitor Guidance in Chronic Kidney Disease

options.text: Cease perindopril because of the reduced eGFR and switch to amlodipine
options.rationale: ACE inhibitors are renoprotective in albuminuric CKD and continued unless serum creatinine rises more than 30 percent or hyperkalaemia develops; switching to a calcium channel blocker loses the renal-protection benefit (Source: KHA-CARI SGLT2 Inhibitor Guidance in Chronic Kidney Disease).
source_refs: KHA-CARI SGLT2 Inhibitor Guidance in Chronic Kidney Disease

options.text: Add oral dulaglutide 1.5 mg weekly injection as a GLP-1 receptor agonist for weight loss
options.rationale: GLP-1 agonists provide cardiovascular and modest renal benefit but the specific gap here is a proven kidney-protective agent for progressive albuminuric CKD, which is the SGLT2 inhibitor class (Source: KHA-CARI SGLT2 Inhibitor Guidance in Chronic Kidney Disease).
source_refs: KHA-CARI SGLT2 Inhibitor Guidance in Chronic Kidney Disease

explanation.summary: SGLT2 inhibitors are now the first-line addition for T2DM with albuminuric CKD because of consistent cardiorenal benefit (slower eGFR decline, reduced hospitalisation for heart failure, reduced cardiovascular death). Australian guidance from KHA-CARI accepts initiation down to eGFR 20 mL/min/1.73 m2 and continuation to dialysis. The main risks are volume depletion, mycotic genital infection, and euglycaemic DKA (particularly if metformin or insulin is reduced peri-operatively). ACE inhibitors are continued unless creatinine rises more than 30 percent or hyperkalaemia develops; metformin is continued at 500 mg twice daily if eGFR falls to 30.
key_points: SGLT2 inhibitors: add for T2DM with eGFR 20 or above with albuminuric CKD
Empagliflozin licensed in AU down to eGFR 20 and continued to dialysis
Watch for euglycaemic DKA and mycotic infection; hold before major surgery
explanation.pearls: SGLT2 inhibitors cause a small expected acute eGFR dip in the first 4 weeks; do not stop the drug for this drop unless it exceeds 30 percent or is accompanied by other markers of AKI.

sources.label: KHA-CARI SGLT2 Inhibitor Guidance in Chronic Kidney Disease
CSANZ Position Statement on SGLT2 Inhibitors
